questions.text:
In 2024, a major international arts and music festival was held in New Zealand, attracting thousands of visitors who spent money on accommodation, food, and transport.

On Graph One below, show the impact on aggregate demand of hosting this international festival. Fully label all changes.
questions.expectedAnswer: AD curve shifts right (AD to AD1) due to increased consumption spending and export receipts from international visitors.
questions.markingGuide: AD shifted to the right and labelled correctly.

questions.text: Explain the impact on inflation of hosting this international arts festival in New Zealand. Refer to Graph One in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: The festival increases consumer spending (C) and export receipts (X) as international visitors spend in NZ, shifting AD right. This increases the price level from PL to PL1, resulting in demand-pull inflation.
questions.markingGuide: Correctly identifies increase in aggregate demand leading to increase in price level (demand-pull inflation) with reference to Graph One.

questions.text:
In early 2024, a shortage of skilled construction workers increased labour costs for New Zealand building companies.

On Graph Two below, show the impact on aggregate supply of rising labour costs for New Zealand businesses.
questions.expectedAnswer: AS curve shifts left (AS to AS1) due to increased costs of production from higher labour costs.
questions.markingGuide: AS curve shifted to the left and labelled correctly.

questions.text: Explain the impact on inflation of rising labour costs for New Zealand businesses. Refer to Graph Two in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Rising labour costs increase costs of production for NZ building companies and businesses that rely on construction, shifting AS left. This increases the price level from PL to PL1, resulting in cost-push inflation.
questions.markingGuide: Identifies decrease in aggregate supply leading to increase in price level (cost-push inflation) with reference to Graph Two.

questions.text: Discuss whether the international arts festival or the rise in labour costs is likely to have had the more significant impact on New Zealand's current inflation rate. Refer to Graphs One and Two in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Rising labour costs likely had a larger impact on inflation because they affect all businesses that employ workers, raising prices across the entire economy persistently. The arts festival's impact on AD was temporary and concentrated in a few regions.
questions.markingGuide: Explains why one factor had greater impact — temporary vs. persistent, localised vs. economy-wide, compares size of price level changes on both graphs.

questions.text: The business cycle shows fluctuations in real GDP over time. On Model One, identify and mark with an X the point that best represents an economic boom.
questions.expectedAnswer: X marked at the peak of the business cycle (highest point above trend growth).
questions.markingGuide: Model labelled correctly — X at the peak/top of the cycle.

questions.text:
State the components of the quantity theory of money.

M:
V: Velocity of circulation
P:
Q:
questions.expectedAnswer: M = Money supply, V = Velocity of circulation, P = Price level, Q = Quantity of goods and services (real output/GDP).
questions.markingGuide: Correctly identifies M (money supply), P (price level), Q (quantity of output/real GDP).

questions.text: Explain why the velocity of circulation is likely to increase during an economic boom.
questions.expectedAnswer: During a boom, consumer and business confidence is high, leading households to spend more freely and borrow more. Money changes hands more frequently, increasing V.
questions.markingGuide: Links boom to higher consumer confidence/spending leading to more frequent transactions, therefore higher V.

questions.text: Assuming all other variables remain constant, use the quantity theory of money to explain how an increase in the velocity of circulation will impact inflation.
questions.expectedAnswer: MV = PQ. If V increases and M and Q are constant, then P must increase proportionally to maintain the equation. Higher V leads to higher P, meaning upward pressure on the price level (inflation).
questions.markingGuide: Explains an increase in P using the equation MV=PQ, showing the proportional relationship between V and P.

questions.text:
Use the quantity theory of money and the business cycle to explain how an economic boom may impact overall inflation.

In your answer, include:
- why real output may increase during a boom
- how the change in velocity of circulation as well as real output will impact the price level in the economy.
questions.expectedAnswer: In a boom, real output (Q) increases as businesses expand production to meet strong demand. Using MV=PQ: V increases (pushes P up) but Q also increases (pushes P down, since more output absorbs spending). The net effect on P depends on relative magnitudes. If V rises faster than Q, inflation accelerates.
questions.markingGuide: Fully explains the competing effects: V increase pushes P up, Q increase pushes P down; integrates business cycle and MV=PQ to assess the net impact.

questions.text:
The graph below shows New Zealand's annual inflation rate from 2018 to 2024.

Define inflation, and identify the year in which NZ experienced the highest inflation rate.
questions.expectedAnswer: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time. The highest rate was in 2022.
questions.markingGuide: Correct definition — must include 'sustained' and 'general price level'. Identifies 2022 as the year with highest inflation from the graph.

questions.text: Explain whether retired people living on a fixed pension would prefer a lower or higher inflation rate.
questions.expectedAnswer: Retired people on a fixed pension would prefer lower inflation because high inflation erodes the purchasing power of their pension. If the pension does not keep pace with rising prices, their real income falls and they can afford fewer goods and services.
questions.markingGuide: Explains why a lower inflation rate is preferred — real income/purchasing power maintained.

questions.text: Explain whether borrowers would prefer a lower or higher inflation rate.
questions.expectedAnswer: Borrowers prefer higher inflation because it reduces the real value of their debt. If the inflation rate exceeds the interest rate on their loan, the purchasing power of the money they owe decreases over time, effectively making their debt cheaper to repay.
questions.markingGuide: Identifies that a higher inflation rate is preferred by borrowers and explains the impact on real value of debt.

questions.text:
The chart below compares annual inflation rates in 2023 for New Zealand, Singapore, and Canada.

Compare and contrast the impact of New Zealand's higher inflation rate on New Zealand importers and exporters trading with Singapore and Canada.
questions.expectedAnswer: NZ exporters are disadvantaged because NZ goods become relatively more expensive compared to Singaporean and Canadian goods, reducing international competitiveness and potentially reducing export volumes. NZ importers benefit because Singaporean and Canadian goods become relatively cheaper compared to NZ goods, meaning imported products cost less in real terms.
questions.markingGuide: Fully explains impact of inflation on both importers AND exporters, comparing/contrasting effects with reference to both trading partners.
